analysis.one_liner: Loosens FDA drug-approval standards and conflict-of-interest rules to speed drugs and devices to market.
analysis.headline: The TREAT Act, introduced by one senator with a single cosponsor, was referred to the Senate health committee and died there without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would restructure the FDA around faster approvals. It would create a Chief Innovation Officer and a Management Review Board that includes representatives of the pharmaceutical, biotechnology, medical device, and food industries and is explicitly exempt from the FDA's conflict-of-interest law. It would make it easier for experts with financial stakes to serve on FDA advisory committees, and it would let the FDA approve drugs for serious or life-threatening diseases based on surrogate measures that are only "reasonably likely" to predict benefit, rather than proof the drug actually helps patients. It would also let companies get parts of their application reviewed before it is complete, and require the FDA to explain in writing why it rejected a drug.
analysis.who_benefits: Pharmaceutical, biotechnology, and medical device companies gain the most: shorter or smaller clinical trials, review of incomplete applications, advisory committees whose members can more easily hold financial interests in the products under review, and a written roadmap of what the FDA needs for approval after a rejection. Patients with serious or life-threatening diseases could also gain earlier access to experimental drugs, though on weaker evidence.

how_it_helps.text: Lets the FDA approve drugs for serious or life-threatening conditions based on a surrogate endpoint 'reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit' — evidence that falls short of showing the drug actually extends life or prevents harm.
Speeds up review by letting the FDA evaluate and begin reviewing pieces of a fast-track application before the sponsor submits a complete one.

Relaxes the conflict-of-interest standard for FDA advisory committee members — from any financial interest that could be affected by the advice, to only a 'direct and predictable' financial interest — and expands the Secretary's power to waive even that restriction.

Creates a Management Review Board that includes at least one representative each from the pharmaceutical, biotechnology, medical device, and food industries, is exempt from the FDA advisory-committee conflict-of-interest statute, and whose recommendations the Secretary must implement within three years unless formally objected to.
Requires the FDA to give drug companies a written explanation of why an application was denied and what data and endpoints would be needed for approval.

analysis.who_pays: Patients prescribed drugs approved on surrogate endpoints would bear the risk that the drugs do not deliver the predicted benefit — the safeguard is post-approval studies that may take years. The public also pays in the form of weakened conflict-of-interest guardrails around FDA decision-making. Taxpayers would fund the new offices and board the bill creates.

drawbacks.text: Approval on a surrogate endpoint that is only 'reasonably likely' to predict benefit means patients could take drugs whose real effect on survival or morbidity is unproven at the time of approval; the check is later post-approval studies, which can fail or drag on.

The bill narrows the definition of a disqualifying financial conflict from any interest 'that could be affected' to one that is 'direct and predictable,' and lets the Secretary waive even that — making it easier for experts with ties to the product under review to vote on FDA advisory committees.
The new Management Review Board is expressly exempt from the FDA's conflict-of-interest statute and reserves seats for representatives of the very industries the FDA regulates.

It creates several new offices and boards — a Chief Innovation Officer, three Chief Medical Policy Officers, a Clinical Informatics Coordinator, and the Management Review Board — adding administrative structure without a dedicated funding source.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients with terminal or untreatable conditions, faster access to experimental drugs is a real benefit, and written denial reasons would give companies useful clarity. But the bill's center of gravity is lowering the bar for industry: weaker evidence standards for approval, easier waivers of conflicts of interest for advisors, and industry-seated management oversight. The patient-access upside is real but conditional and speculative; the regulatory loosening is certain. On balance, the bill was designed to serve the regulated industries first.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Health Committee, which never took it up before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Kay Hagan introduced the bill on February 15, 2012, with remarks in the Congressional Record.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — is recorded in the bill's complete action history before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, a Democrat.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients who rely on the FDA's stricter evidence standards are better off that this version never became law, since its weaker approval criteria and loosened conflict-of-interest rules never took effect through this bill; drug makers are worse off only to the extent that this vehicle died, as the same ideas were pushed again in later Congresses.

for.name: Sen. Kay R. Hagan
for.role: U.S. Senator from North Carolina; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; referred it to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.

for.name: Biotechnology and pharmaceutical industry groups
for.role: Regulated industries seeking faster FDA approvals
for.what_they_did: Backed the bill's push to speed drug approvals and ease regulatory requirements; the bill itself builds in formal roles for regulated industries, including reserved seats and mandated consultation on the new Management Review Board.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats supported the bill on the record — one sponsor and one cosponsor — and no one ever voted on it, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would let these companies win approval for serious-disease drugs with shorter or smaller trials based on surrogate endpoints, start review before applications are complete, and get written denial roadmaps. Desperate patients would gain earlier access, but the certainty of faster, easier market entry accrues to the companies while the risk of unproven drugs falls on patients.

The bill would put a Chief Medical Policy Officer inside the device center, require the FDA to solicit industry input on review policy, and loosen conflict-of-interest rules for advisory panels that review device applications.

The bill reserves a board seat for a food-industry representative and mandates meetings where food, cosmetic, and supplement industries give input on FDA management changes — giving them a formal voice over how their regulator is run.

industries.industry: FDA advisory committee experts with industry financial ties
industries.note: By narrowing the disqualifying conflict standard and expanding waivers, the bill would make it easier for experts with financial interests in a product's outcome to participate in — and vote on — the committees that recommend its approval.
